items.name: c05
items.direction: Narrate this as a popular, witty long-form history YouTube documentary about India. The Narrator is a deep, warm, confident storyteller: relaxed and conversational, curious, lightly funny, with a short comic pause before each punchline and before chapter turns. Chars voices funny cartoon characters (a cheeky time-traveller, city inspectors, brick-makers, engineers, kings, emperors, sultans, merchants, soldiers): short, punchy, expressive, following the bracketed style tags. Pronounce Indian names and places naturally, the way an Indian speaker would. VOICE IDENTITY (most important): the Narrator is always the same person: a low, warm baritone documentary host. Keep his voice identity and natural speaking pitch the same from the first line to the last, so it never sounds like a different or younger narrator. Emotion is welcome: show it freely through emphasis, energy, pace, louder and softer moments and dramatic pauses, as a real storyteller would. Never whisper or go breathy.
lines: For the next few centuries, India was ruled by many kingdoms at once. And in many ways, it got richer.
The Kushans, who came from Central Asia, built an empire across the north. Their king Kanishka became a great patron of Buddhism. Absorb.
In the south, ships sailed with the monsoon winds to Egypt and Rome, loaded with pepper, cotton cloth and gems.
So much Roman gold flowed to India that the Roman writer Pliny complained about it. He grumbled that India drained Rome of fifty million sesterces every year.
[checking a coin] The Golden Bird. Already collecting gold.
Then, around three hundred twenty CE, a new family united the north again: the Guptas. Stitch.
The Gupta age is often called India's classical age. And the reason is not its battles. It's its ideas.
The poet Kalidasa wrote plays and poems still performed today.
The mathematician Aryabhata, at just twenty-three, wrote that the Earth spins on its own axis... about a thousand years before Copernicus.
He worked out pi to four decimal places: three point one four one six.
And Indian mathematicians were developing the number system you use every day: nine digits, plus a place for nothing.
Just over a century later, the mathematician Brahmagupta wrote the rules for zero as a number in its own right. Add, subtract, multiply.
These numerals travelled to the Arab world and then to Europe. Which is why we call them... Arabic numerals.
[confused] So the sky turns around the Earth every night?
No. The Earth turns. The sky stays still.
[looking down at his feet] Then why am I not dizzy?
[patiently] I'll explain tomorrow. If the Earth is still here.
Students came from across Asia to study at Nalanda, one of the world's earliest great universities, with thousands of students and a library so big, it filled several buildings.
Even the iron got better. The Iron Pillar of Delhi, made in the Gupta age, has stood in the open for about sixteen hundred years... and has barely rusted.
[knocking on the pillar] My bicycle rusted in one monsoon.
But in the five hundreds, raiders called the Huna swept in from Central Asia. The Gupta Empire cracked. Shatter. Again.
In the south, though, the story was just getting started.

The Chola kings of Tamil Nadu built one of the greatest navies in Asian history. Rajaraja the First built the vast Brihadeeswarar Temple at Thanjavur, finished around ten ten. Its tower is about sixty-six metres tall.
His son, Rajendra, sent his fleet across the Bay of Bengal to attack the mighty Srivijaya kingdom in Sumatra and Malaya.
[looking at a map] An Indian navy. Raiding Southeast Asia. A thousand years ago.
But in the north, things were about to change. A powerful sultan had just learned how rich India's temples were.
His name was Mahmud of Ghazni, from today's Afghanistan. Starting around the year one thousand, he raided north India again and again. Around seventeen times.
He came for gold. His raiders looted cities and temples, including the famous temple of Somnath in Gujarat, in ten twenty-six. Then he went home.
Mahmud didn't stay to rule. But about a hundred and fifty years later, another invader did: Muhammad of Ghor.
In eleven ninety-one, at Tarain, near Delhi, he met the Rajput king Prithviraj Chauhan. And Prithviraj won. Ghori was wounded and fled.
A year later, Ghori came back with a bigger army. Same battlefield. This time, Prithviraj lost.
[wincing] Rule one of history: if you beat someone, make sure they don't come back next year.
In twelve oh six, Ghori's general Qutb ud-Din Aibak became the first ruler of the Delhi Sultanate. He began the tallest brick minaret in the world: the Qutb Minar.
Around the same time, according to later chronicles, raiders led by Bakhtiyar Khalji attacked Nalanda, and the great university was ruined.
For the next three hundred years, five different dynasties would rule from Delhi.
One sultan, Alauddin Khalji, beat back several Mongol invasions. Unlike China, Persia and Russia, India was never conquered by the Mongols.
He also tried something very modern: price controls. He fixed the price of grain, horses, cloth, even slaves in the markets of Delhi, and punished cheating shopkeepers harshly.
[taking notes] The first price regulator. Strict. Very, very strict.
Then came the strangest sultan of all: Muhammad bin Tughlaq. Clever, well-read... and full of big ideas.
In thirteen twenty-seven, he decided to move the capital from Delhi to Daulatabad, about a thousand kilometres south. And he ordered much of Delhi's population to move with him.
[cheerful] Great news! We are moving the capital. Everybody pack.
[reading the map] It's... forty days' walk.
[whispering] A few years later, he moves everyone back.
He also issued copper and brass coins and declared them worth the same as silver.
Within months, people were making their own coins at home. Huge piles of fake money. He had to buy them all back with real silver.
[shaking his head] Great idea. Five hundred years too early.
In thirteen ninety-eight, the Central Asian conqueror Timur sacked Delhi. The city took a century to recover. Shatter.
Meanwhile, in the south, a powerful Hindu empire was rising: Vijayanagara, with its capital at Hampi. Foreign visitors said it was as big as Rome, and full of diamonds and horses.
But here's the thing about the Sultanate years. Something new was also being made.

Persian and Indian builders mixed their styles in arches, domes and minarets. The poet Amir Khusrau wrote in a mix of Persian and the local speech, and is traditionally credited with shaping qawwali music.
Out of the bazaars and army camps, a whole new language grew: what would become Urdu, and close cousin to Hindi.
[smiling] India doesn't just get invaded. It gets... remixed.
In fifteen twenty-six, a young prince from Central Asia rode down from Kabul. He had lost his homeland more than once. He was looking for a new one.
His great-great-great-grandfather was Timur. And on his mother's side, he was descended from Genghis Khan.

lines: His name was Babur. And at Panipat, north of Delhi, he faced the Sultan Ibrahim Lodi, who had a far bigger army and around a hundred elephants.
But Babur brought something new to India: cannons and guns. The elephants panicked. In a single day, the Sultanate was gone.
Babur founded the Mughal Empire. Stitch, again.
He also wrote a remarkable memoir, the Baburnama. And honestly? He wasn't that impressed with India.
He complained there were no good horses, no good grapes, and no good melons.
[proudly] Your Majesty, the finest mangoes in Hindustan!
[writing gloomily] Day four hundred. Still no melons.
Babur ruled for only four years. His son Humayun lost the whole empire to an Afghan general, Sher Shah Suri.
Sher Shah ruled for just five years, but he was brilliant. He improved the great road from Bengal to the northwest, later called the Grand Trunk Road, with rest houses and wells along the way.
And he issued a new silver coin. He called it the rupiya.
[holding up a coin] The rupee. Started by the guy who kicked the Mughals out.
Humayun came back fifteen years later and took Delhi again. A few months later, he slipped on the stairs of his library and died.
His son was thirteen years old. His name was Akbar.
In fifteen fifty-six, at a second battle at Panipat, Akbar's army defeated the general Hemu. And over the next fifty years, Akbar built one of the richest empires on Earth.
Akbar's secret weapon was not cannons. It was including people.
He made alliances with the Rajput kingdoms, many through marriage, and gave Rajput princes high posts in his army.
He scrapped the jizya, a tax paid by non-Muslims. And his finance minister, Raja Todar Mal, built a careful system for measuring land and setting taxes.
Akbar could barely read. Yet he collected a huge library, and had books read aloud to him every day.
At his new city, Fatehpur Sikri, he built a hall where Muslim, Hindu, Jain, Zoroastrian and Christian scholars debated religion in front of him.
[whispering] The debates got so heated, the Emperor had to play referee.

Not everyone accepted Akbar. The Rajput ruler of Mewar, Maharana Pratap, refused to submit, and fought Akbar's army at Haldighati in fifteen seventy-six. He kept resisting from the hills for the rest of his life.
Still, by the time Akbar died in sixteen oh five, the Mughal Empire was enormous. And it was only getting richer.
Remember the hook? That quarter of the world's economy? That was the India his grandson would rule.
[checking his watch, excited] Now we're getting to the gold.
Akbar's son Jahangir loved art, gardens and wine, and his court painters made some of the most beautiful miniatures ever painted.
The real power behind his throne was often his wife, Nur Jahan. She issued orders, minted coins in her own name... and once, the story goes, shot a tiger from the back of an elephant.
[impressed] Coins with her name on them. That's real power.
Then came Shah Jahan. And under him, the Mughal Empire reached its peak of wealth and show.
He sat on the Peacock Throne, covered in gold and jewels. It reportedly took seven years to make.
And when his favourite wife, Mumtaz Mahal, died giving birth to their fourteenth child, he built her a tomb on the river at Agra.
Around twenty thousand workers and craftsmen, more than twenty years. White marble from Rajasthan, inlaid with stones from across Asia.
In this age, India was one of the richest places on Earth. Indian cotton cloth dressed half the world. Silver poured in from Europe to pay for it.
This was the Golden Bird at its brightest. Shine.
[pointing at the Taj] Remember the quarter of the world's economy? You're looking at it.
But Shah Jahan's sons fought a brutal war for the throne. The winner was Aurangzeb.
He had his brothers killed... and locked his own father inside Agra Fort, where, the story goes, Shah Jahan spent his last years gazing across the river at the Taj.
[not turning] Is my son coming to visit?
[sighing] Regards. I gave him an empire.
Aurangzeb ruled for almost fifty years, and pushed the empire to its largest size ever. Almost the whole subcontinent.
But he spent the last twenty-five years of his life fighting in the Deccan, in the south. And he brought back the jizya tax on non-Muslims.
His toughest enemy was a young Maratha leader from the hills near Pune: Shivaji.
Shivaji was a master of fast raids and hill forts. In sixteen sixty-six, he was invited to Aurangzeb's court in Agra... and placed under house arrest.
The story goes that he escaped by hiding inside giant baskets of sweets, sent out of the house as gifts.
[eyeing a basket of laddoos] Next time I'm checking every mithai box.
In sixteen seventy-four, Shivaji was crowned king, and the Maratha kingdom kept growing long after his death.
When Aurangzeb died in seventeen oh seven, the empire began to crack. Governors became kings. The Marathas spread across the centre of India.
And in seventeen thirty-nine, the Persian ruler Nadir Shah marched in and sacked Delhi.
He carried home the Peacock Throne... and a diamond the size of a small egg: the Koh-i-Noor. Shatter.
[checking his empty pockets] The Golden Bird is losing feathers.
Meanwhile, quietly, along the coasts, there was a different kind of visitor. They didn't come with armies. They came with account books.

lines: On the last day of sixteen hundred, Queen Elizabeth the First gave a charter to a group of London merchants: the East India Company.
They were not the first Europeans here. The Portuguese had arrived by sea a century earlier, and the Dutch and French were here too.
At first, the Company just wanted to trade. Pepper. Cotton. Indigo. Tea. It set up trading posts at Surat, Madras, Bombay and Calcutta.
Bombay, by the way, came to England as part of a royal wedding dowry, when a Portuguese princess married King Charles the Second.
[shocked] Imagine getting Mumbai as a wedding gift.
But to protect its trade, the Company hired soldiers. Then more soldiers. Then a lot more.
By the early eighteen hundreds, the Company's private army in India was about two hundred thousand strong. Bigger than the British Army itself.
Excellent. And what's this line? "Cannons. Elephants. Regiments."
We're a trading company. Why do we have an army?
In seventeen fifty-seven, at Plassey in Bengal, the Company's commander Robert Clive faced the Nawab of Bengal, Siraj ud-Daulah.
Clive's army was much smaller. But he had secretly made a deal with the Nawab's own commander, Mir Jafar. When the battle began, much of the Nawab's army simply... stood still.
[facepalm] One of the most important battles in Indian history. Won by a betrayal.
Within a few years, the Company won the right to collect the taxes of Bengal, one of the richest provinces in the world.
A company now ruled millions of people. And its first priority was profit.
In seventeen seventy, a terrible famine struck Bengal. Some estimates say up to a third of the population died. Tax collection barely slowed.

Not everyone gave in. In the south, the kingdom of Mysore, under Hyder Ali and his son Tipu Sultan, fought the Company in four wars. Its army used iron-cased rockets so effective that the British studied them and built their own.
Tipu died defending his capital in seventeen ninety-nine.
In the Punjab, Maharaja Ranjit Singh built a strong Sikh empire and kept the Company out for forty years. He even owned the Koh-i-Noor.

But after he died, the Company fought two wars with the Sikhs. In eighteen forty-nine, it took the Punjab... and the diamond went to Queen Victoria. It is still in London today, and India has asked for it back.
[sighing] The diamond's been on quite a journey.
By the eighteen-fifties, the Company controlled most of India, directly or through puppet kings.
And the soldiers it relied on most, the sepoys, were Indian. That was about to matter. A lot.
In eighteen fifty-seven, the Company gave its Indian soldiers a new rifle. To load it, you had to bite open a paper cartridge.
A rumour spread like fire: the cartridges were greased with cow and pig fat. Offensive to both Hindus and Muslims.
At Meerut, in May, soldiers who refused the cartridges were jailed. Their comrades rose up, freed them, and marched to Delhi.
There, they declared the old, powerless Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, the ruler of India again.
[nervously winding his watch] The Company has a problem.
The revolt spread across north India. In Jhansi, a young queen, Rani Lakshmibai, led her troops into battle on horseback, and died fighting.
The British crushed the rising with terrible brutality. Whole villages were burned. Rebels were tied to cannons and blown apart.
Bahadur Shah Zafar was exiled to Rangoon in Burma. The Mughal dynasty, after three hundred and thirty years, was over.
And the British government decided the Company could not be trusted with India anymore. In eighteen fifty-eight, the British Crown took over directly. The British Raj had begun.
Your Majesty, India is now ruled by the Crown.
[eyeing the crown] Then I shall need a new title.
She did get it, eventually. In eighteen seventy-six, Queen Victoria was proclaimed Empress of India.
Under the Raj, India got railways, telegraph lines, universities and a new class of English-educated Indians.
The first passenger train ran in eighteen fifty-three, from Bombay to Thane. Remember the railway that buried the bricks of Harappa? Same era.
But the railways were built mainly to carry raw cotton to the ports, and British factory cloth back in.
India, once the world's great cloth-maker, now bought its cloth from Manchester.
And famines kept coming. In the Great Famine of eighteen seventy-six, millions died, while grain was still being exported.
An Indian thinker named Dadabhai Naoroji added up the numbers and gave it a name: the drain of wealth. Money flowing out of India, year after year.
Remember that quarter of the world's economy? By nineteen fifty, India's share had fallen to about four percent.
[quietly] The shop wasn't just unlocked. It was emptied.
But the same schools and newspapers the British built gave Indians the tools to fight back. Not with swords this time. With ideas.

lines: In eighteen eighty-five, a group of educated Indians founded the Indian National Congress. At first, they just asked politely for more say.
In nineteen oh five, the British split Bengal in two. Bengal exploded in protest. People burned British cloth and bought Indian goods only: Swadeshi.
In nineteen fifteen, a lawyer came home from South Africa, where he had spent twenty years fighting discrimination against Indians.
He wore simple clothes and spoke softly. His name was Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi. People came to call him Mahatma, "great soul".
His weapon was satyagraha: holding on to the truth, and resisting without violence.
[puzzled] Fighting an empire without fighting. Let's see how this goes.
In nineteen nineteen, in Amritsar, thousands of people gathered peacefully in a walled garden called Jallianwala Bagh.
A British general, Reginald Dyer, blocked the only exit and ordered his troops to fire into the crowd. They fired until they ran out of bullets.
The official count said three hundred and seventy-nine dead. Indian estimates were over a thousand.
After Amritsar, millions of Indians who had trusted the British stopped trusting them.
Gandhi called on India to stop cooperating: leave British schools, courts and jobs, and burn foreign cloth.
In nineteen thirty, he chose an unlikely target: salt. The British taxed it, and Indians were banned from making their own.
[stern] Mr Gandhi, what exactly are you doing?
[holding up a pinch of salt] Picking up salt.
[calmly] Then arrest me. And the thousands behind me.
[looking at the crowd, gulping] I'll need a bigger notebook.
The Salt March covered about three hundred and eighty kilometres in twenty-four days. Newspapers around the world followed every step.
Not everyone believed in non-violence. Young revolutionaries like Bhagat Singh took up arms. He was hanged in nineteen thirty-one, at just twenty-three, and became a hero across India.
And Dr B R Ambedkar, born into a so-called "untouchable" caste, fought for the rights of India's most oppressed communities.
When the Second World War came, about two and a half million Indian soldiers fought for Britain. The largest volunteer army in history.
Meanwhile, Subhas Chandra Bose tried another path: he raised the Indian National Army with Japan's help, to fight the British from the east.
In nineteen forty-two, Gandhi gave Britain a simple message: Quit India. Almost the entire Congress leadership was thrown in jail.
In nineteen forty-three, a famine in Bengal killed around three million people.
By the end of the war, Britain was broke and exhausted. And it could no longer hold on to India.
Freedom was coming. But it was not coming whole.
As freedom came closer, the deep split between the Congress and the Muslim League, led by Muhammad Ali Jinnah, could not be bridged. The League demanded a separate country for Muslims: Pakistan.
In the end, Britain agreed to divide the land.
The border was drawn by a British lawyer, Cyril Radcliffe, who had never been to India. He was given about five weeks.
[horrified] Five weeks. To divide four hundred million people.
At midnight on the fifteenth of August, nineteen forty-seven, India became free.

In Delhi, Jawaharlal Nehru, the first Prime Minister, told the assembly that India had made a tryst with destiny. At the stroke of midnight, while the world slept, India would awake to life and freedom.
But the border was only announced two days later. And across Punjab and Bengal, millions of people suddenly found themselves on the "wrong" side.
What followed was one of the largest migrations in human history. Somewhere between ten and twenty million people were forced to leave their homes.
And there was terrible violence on both sides. Estimates of the dead range from two hundred thousand to two million.
[quietly] Every one of those numbers was a family.
Gandhi spent Independence Day not in Delhi, but in Calcutta, fasting to stop the killing.
Five months later, on the thirtieth of January, nineteen forty-eight, he was shot dead in Delhi by a Hindu extremist.
And India still had another enormous problem. More than five hundred and sixty princely states, each ruled by its own maharaja or nawab, had to decide where to go.
The man in charge was the Home Minister, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, with his right-hand man, V P Menon.
[grandly] My family has ruled here for three hundred years.
[calmly] And India would be honoured to keep you comfortable for three hundred more.
[sighing, picking up the pen] You make it sound so easy.

Most rulers signed. Hyderabad held out until the Indian army moved in, in nineteen forty-eight. Kashmir's ruler signed after raiders from Pakistan invaded, and the first war between India and Pakistan began.
Patel became known as the Iron Man of India. Stitch. Bigger than any empire before.
Then India wrote its rules. A committee led by Dr Ambedkar drafted the Constitution: the longest written constitution of any country.
It came into force on the twenty-sixth of January, nineteen fifty. Republic Day.
And it did something many rich democracies took centuries to do. It gave every adult the vote, from day one. Rich or poor, man or woman, of every caste and religion.
In the first election, in nineteen fifty-one, about a hundred and seventy million people were eligible to vote. Most of them could not read. So each party had a picture symbol.
[grinning] The biggest election the world had ever seen. Run on pictures.
The Golden Bird was free. Now it had to learn to fly again.

lines: The young republic had a rough start. India lost a border war with China in nineteen sixty-two, and fought Pakistan in nineteen sixty-five.
In the mid-sixties, India was so short of food that it depended on grain shipments from America.
Then came the Green Revolution. New high-yield wheat and rice, irrigation and fertiliser. Within a decade, India was growing enough to feed itself.
[holding a bag of rice] From begging for grain to feeding a billion. Not bad.
In nineteen seventy-one, India backed the independence struggle in East Pakistan, and won a short war. A new country was born: Bangladesh.
In nineteen seventy-five, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi declared an Emergency. Elections were suspended, opposition leaders jailed, newspapers censored.
But when she finally called elections in nineteen seventy-seven, the voters threw her out.
[nodding] The voters remembered the picture symbols.
She came back to power in nineteen eighty. In nineteen eighty-four, she was assassinated, and terrible violence against Sikhs followed in Delhi and other cities.
For most of these years, India's economy was tightly controlled. You needed government permission to make almost anything. People called it the Licence Raj.
In nineteen ninety-one, India almost ran out of money. Its foreign reserves could pay for only about three weeks of imports.
To get an emergency loan, the government flew forty-seven tonnes of gold to the Bank of England.
[reading] Cargo: forty-seven tonnes of gold. Destination: London.
[confused] Wait... didn't the British take enough already?
[sighing] This time, we're getting it back.

That crisis forced a revolution. Prime Minister P V Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Manmohan Singh opened the economy: lower taxes on imports, private companies welcome, foreign investment allowed.
Then India's growth took off. Software companies in Bengaluru and Hyderabad began serving the whole world.
In two thousand fourteen, India reached Mars on its very first try. The mission cost about seventy-four million dollars. Less than the Hollywood space film Gravity.
[laughing] Cheaper than a movie about space. Actually in space.
In two thousand twenty-three, Chandrayaan-3 became the first spacecraft to land near the Moon's south pole. That same year, India became the most populous country on Earth.
Narendra Modi has been Prime Minister since two thousand fourteen. His supporters point to new roads and airports, digital payments used by hundreds of millions, and fast growth.
His critics worry about jobs, inequality, and pressure on the press and on religious minorities.
And today, India is the world's fifth-largest economy in dollars. The IMF expects it to pass Japan in two thousand twenty-seven. Measured by what money can actually buy, it's already third.
So let's look back at the loop.
The Indus cities stitched together, shone, and went silent. The Mauryas stitched the land together, shone, and shattered. Then the Guptas. Then the Sultans. Then the Mughals.
Every time, outsiders marched in. And every time, India absorbed them. Their food, their words, their buildings, their gods all became part of the same story.
[winding his watch] Stitch. Shine. Shatter. Absorb.
Three hundred years ago, India made about a quarter of everything in the world. By nineteen fifty, about four percent.
The question is no longer whether the Golden Bird can fly again. It's whether this time, India can shine without the shatter.
[looking up] I've seen how this story usually goes. But I've also seen this land surprise everyone. Many times.
What do you think? Can India break the loop?
[checking his watch, grinning] Next stop: China. They have a loop of their own.
